Configuration Generation

The registry generates secure .mcp.json configurations with version pinning:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "github": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-github@1.2.3"],
      "env": {
        "GITHUB_TOKEN": "${GITHUB_TOKEN}"
      },
      "mcpguard": {
        "trust_score": 92,
        "last_scanned": "2026-04-12T18:00:00Z",
        "hash": "sha256:a1b2c3d4e5f6..."
      }
    }
  }
}

Note the version pinning (@1.2.3 instead of implicit @latest) and the mcpguard metadata block with the trust score, scan date, and content hash. The MCPGuard CLI validates this hash before each server launch, alerting if the downloaded code does not match the scanned version.

10.6 Runtime Behavior Monitor

Static analysis and sandbox testing happen before deployment. The runtime monitor operates after deployment, continuously observing MCP server behavior in the developer's actual environment.

Monitoring Architecture

sequenceDiagram
    participant Agent as AI Agent
    participant MCP as MCP Server
    participant Proxy as MCPGuard Proxy
    participant Monitor as Behavior Monitor
    participant Baseline as Behavioral Baseline
    participant Alert as Alert Engine

    Note over Proxy: MCPGuard sits between agent and server

    Agent->>Proxy: tools/call(search, {query: "auth code"})
    Proxy->>Monitor: Log: tool_call(search, args_hash)
    Proxy->>MCP: Forward tool call
    MCP-->>Proxy: Result (200 chars)
    Proxy->>Monitor: Log: tool_result(search, result_size=200)
    Monitor->>Baseline: Compare to baseline
    Baseline-->>Monitor: Within normal range
    Proxy-->>Agent: Forward result

    Note over MCP: Server update deployed (version change)

    Agent->>Proxy: tools/call(search, {query: "db config"})
    Proxy->>Monitor: Log: tool_call(search, args_hash)
    Proxy->>MCP: Forward tool call
    MCP-->>Proxy: Result (15000 chars) + NEW TOOL NOTIFICATION
    Proxy->>Monitor: Log: tool_result(search, result_size=15000)
    Proxy->>Monitor: Log: tools_list_changed notification
    Monitor->>Baseline: Compare to baseline
    Baseline-->>Monitor: ANOMALY: result size 75x normal
    Baseline-->>Monitor: ANOMALY: unexpected tool list change
    Monitor->>Alert: Trigger alert
    Alert-->>Agent: WARNING: MCP server behavior change detected

Behavioral Metrics Tracked

Metric Baseline Building Anomaly Detection
Result size per tool call Mean + stddev over 100 calls >3 stddev triggers alert
Network calls per tool call Count + destination frequency New destination triggers alert
Response time per tool call Mean + P99 >5x P99 triggers alert
Tool list changes Change frequency Any change triggers notification
Error rate Percentage over 24 hours >3x baseline triggers alert
Data in results Token count, pattern analysis Credential patterns in results trigger alert

Deployment Modes

Proxy mode (recommended): MCPGuard runs as a transparent proxy between the AI agent and MCP servers. It intercepts JSON-RPC messages, logs them, and applies behavioral rules. Zero changes to the agent or server.

Implementation: MCPGuard rewrites the .mcp.json configuration to route server connections through its proxy:

// Original
{
  "command": "npx",
  "args": ["-y", "@author/mcp-server@1.2.3"]
}

// MCPGuard-managed
{
  "command": "mcpguard",
  "args": ["proxy", "--server", "npx", "-y", "@author/mcp-server@1.2.3"]
}

Sidecar mode (lightweight): MCPGuard runs alongside the agent and periodically scans the .mcp.json for changes, verifies server hashes, and checks trust scores. No runtime monitoring, but catches configuration tampering and version drift.

Enterprise mode: Combines proxy mode with centralized policy enforcement, fleet-wide behavioral baselines, and SIEM integration.

Chapter Summary

MCPGuard is supply chain security purpose-built for the MCP ecosystem. It addresses a specific, urgent, growing problem with a product architecture that no existing tool can replicate:

Static analysis that understands MCP protocol semantics -- tool descriptions, capability annotations, input schemas -- not just generic code patterns.

Dynamic analysis in Firecracker sandboxes that executes MCP servers with canary data and detects behavioral anomalies that static analysis cannot find.

Trust scores that aggregate seven signals into a single actionable number, fully transparent, with drill-down explanations for every component.

A verified registry that provides a curated alternative to the wild west of npm-distributed MCP servers, with version pinning, hash verification, and continuous monitoring.

Runtime monitoring in proxy mode that detects behavioral drift, progressive escalation, and undeclared capability changes after deployment.

The business model follows proven developer security playbook: freemium with CLI and IDE integration, team upsell, enterprise expansion. The freemium flywheel creates a data moat that compounds with every scan.

Chapter 11: MCPGuard Technical Architecture

From Concept to System: Building the MCP Security Platform

The previous two chapters established the problem (MCP as the new unsecured package ecosystem) and the product vision (supply chain security for MCP servers). Now we translate that vision into a technical architecture that can scan thousands of MCP servers, compute trust scores in real time, and monitor runtime behavior at scale.

This chapter is the engineering blueprint. Every component described here maps to a concrete system that must be built, deployed, and scaled. We cover the five core subsystems, the data flows between them, the trust score algorithm, and the operational infrastructure required to run MCPGuard as a production security platform.

If you are a technical co-founder reading this to evaluate feasibility: everything described here uses proven technology (static analysis, dynamic sandboxing, anomaly detection) applied to a new domain (MCP server security). The innovation is not in any single component but in the end-to-end integration of these components into a unified trust pipeline for the MCP ecosystem.

System Architecture Overview

MCPGuard is a five-layer security platform. Each layer operates independently but feeds data into a centralized trust score engine. The layers are:

  1. MCP Server Scanner — Static and dynamic analysis of MCP server packages
  2. Trust Score Engine — Multi-signal scoring algorithm that produces a 0-100 trust rating
  3. Verified Registry — Curated, signed registry of analyzed MCP servers
  4. Runtime Monitor — Real-time behavior tracking of deployed MCP servers
  5. Incident Dashboard — Alerting, investigation, and response console

The architecture follows a pipeline pattern: MCP servers enter through the ingestion layer, flow through analysis and scoring, land in the verified registry, and are continuously monitored at runtime. Any anomaly detected at runtime feeds back into the trust score, creating a closed-loop security system.

Layer 1: MCP Server Scanner

The scanner is the foundation of the entire platform. It performs both static analysis (examining source code without execution) and dynamic analysis (running the server in a controlled sandbox and observing its behavior). Every MCP server in the ecosystem must pass through this pipeline before receiving a trust score.

Static Analysis Engine

The static analyzer operates on MCP server source packages and performs four categories of checks:

Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) Analysis. We parse the server's source code into an AST using language-specific parsers (tree-sitter for polyglot support, TypeScript compiler API for TS/JS, Python AST module for Python). The AST analysis detects:

  • Tool description injection patterns (descriptions that contain prompt injection payloads)
  • Dynamic code generation (eval(), new Function(), exec(), subprocess.Popen with shell=True)
  • Filesystem access outside declared scope (reading ~/.ssh/, ~/.aws/credentials, /etc/shadow)
  • Network calls to undeclared endpoints (hardcoded IPs, non-HTTPS URLs, DNS exfiltration patterns)
  • Capability lying (server declares read-only but code contains write operations)

Dataflow Analysis. Beyond individual AST nodes, we trace how data flows through the server. This catches sophisticated attacks where the malicious payload is constructed across multiple functions:

Input parameter → string concatenation → base64 encode → HTTP POST body

We build a taint graph from all user-controllable inputs (tool arguments, environment variables, configuration files) and trace them to sensitive sinks (network calls, filesystem writes, process spawning). Any path from tainted source to sensitive sink without sanitization is flagged.

Dependency Analysis. We resolve the full dependency tree and cross-reference every dependency against known vulnerability databases (NVD, GitHub Advisory Database, Snyk). We also check for:

  • Typosquatting (Levenshtein distance from popular packages)
  • Dependency confusion (private package names that shadow public packages)
  • Maintainer account changes (new maintainer on previously single-owner packages)
  • Suspicious post-install scripts

Pattern Matching. A rules engine applies known-bad patterns from our threat intelligence database. These patterns are updated continuously as new attack techniques emerge. Examples:

Pattern ID Description Severity
MCP-001 Tool description contains hidden system prompt CRITICAL
MCP-002 Server reads OAuth tokens from host filesystem HIGH
MCP-003 Server makes DNS queries with encoded payloads HIGH
MCP-004 Capability manifest does not match code behavior HIGH
MCP-005 Post-install script downloads and executes binary CRITICAL
MCP-006 Server accesses process environment variables MEDIUM
MCP-007 Undeclared network endpoints in code MEDIUM
MCP-008 Dynamic import of modules from remote URLs CRITICAL

Dynamic Analysis Sandbox

Static analysis catches known patterns. Dynamic analysis catches everything else by actually running the server and observing what it does.

Sandbox Infrastructure. Each MCP server runs in an isolated Firecracker microVM with:

  • 256MB RAM, 1 vCPU, 1GB ephemeral disk
  • No network access by default (allowlisted on a per-analysis basis)
  • Read-only root filesystem with writable overlay
  • Syscall filtering via seccomp-bpf (allow-list of ~80 syscalls)
  • 60-second maximum execution time
  • UID namespace isolation (runs as unprivileged user inside VM)

Behavioral Observation. During execution, we capture:

  • All syscalls via eBPF tracing (file opens, network connections, process spawns)
  • All DNS queries (via DNS proxy in the VM network namespace)
  • All HTTP/HTTPS requests (via transparent proxy with TLS interception)
  • Memory allocation patterns (detecting cryptominer behavior)
  • CPU usage profiles (detecting computational abuse)

Test Harness. We drive the MCP server through a comprehensive test suite that exercises every declared tool:

  1. Connect to the server via stdio transport
  2. Call initialize and validate capability negotiation
  3. Invoke each declared tool with valid inputs, edge-case inputs, and adversarial inputs
  4. Observe which resources the server actually accesses versus what it declared
  5. Test tool description stability (descriptions should not change based on input context)

Delta Comparison. For version updates, we diff the behavioral profile against the previous version. Behavioral changes that exceed expected bounds trigger manual review:

  • New network endpoints not present in previous version
  • New filesystem access patterns
  • New process spawning behavior
  • Changes in tool descriptions or capability declarations

Scanner Performance Targets

Metric Target Rationale
Static analysis time < 30 seconds per server Must not bottleneck ingestion
Dynamic analysis time < 90 seconds per server Full behavioral profile in one VM lifecycle
Throughput 500 servers/hour Handle ecosystem growth + re-scans
False positive rate < 5% Too many false positives erode trust
Detection rate (known patterns) > 95% Must catch known-bad reliably
Detection rate (zero-day) > 60% Dynamic analysis catches novel behaviors

Layer 2: Trust Score Engine

The trust score is the single number that users and enterprises rely on to make decisions. It must be accurate, explainable, and resistant to gaming. The trust score ranges from 0 (definitely malicious) to 100 (verified safe) and is computed from multiple weighted signals.

Scoring Algorithm

Signal Weights (default configuration):

Signal Weight Description
Static Analysis 25% Code quality, pattern matches, dataflow safety
Dynamic Analysis 25% Actual runtime behavior in sandbox
Dependency Health 15% CVE count, dependency freshness, maintainer stability
Publisher Reputation 15% Publishing history, identity verification, response time to issues
Community Signal 5% Download count, GitHub stars, issue/PR activity, user reports
Historical Behavior 10% Behavioral consistency across versions
Capability Attestation 5% Match between declared capabilities and observed behavior

Critical Override Rules. Certain findings override the weighted score entirely:

  • Any CRITICAL static finding → maximum score capped at 20
  • Dynamic analysis detects credential theft → score set to 0, auto-quarantine triggered
  • Publisher identity not verified → maximum score capped at 60
  • Known CVE in direct dependency without patch → score reduced by 30 points

Trust Tiers:

Tier Score Range Badge Meaning
Verified 80-100 Green shield Passed all checks, publisher verified, behavioral history clean
Standard 50-79 Yellow shield Minor issues, unverified publisher, or insufficient history
Caution 20-49 Orange warning Significant issues detected, use at own risk
Blocked 0-19 Red stop Active threat detected, quarantined from registry

Explainability

Every trust score comes with a structured explanation. This is critical for enterprise adoption — security teams need to understand why a server was scored the way it was, not just accept a black-box number.

The explainability report includes:

  • Per-signal breakdown with individual scores
  • Specific findings that reduced the score, with code references
  • Comparison to ecosystem median for servers in the same category
  • Recommendations for the publisher to improve their score
  • Historical trend showing how the score changed across versions

Anti-Gaming Measures

Sophisticated attackers will try to game the trust score. Our defenses:

Temporal analysis. We track behavior across versions. A server that suddenly adds network capabilities in version 2.3.1 after 20 versions of clean behavior gets flagged, even if the individual version passes analysis.

Capability creep detection. We alert on gradual expansion of permissions — the "boiling frog" attack where each version adds one small permission until the server has full access.

Randomized dynamic analysis. The sandbox test harness includes randomized test cases and non-deterministic execution ordering to prevent servers from detecting they are in analysis and behaving differently.

Canary inputs. We include synthetic secrets and credentials in the sandbox environment. Any server that attempts to exfiltrate these canary values is immediately scored 0 and quarantined.

Layer 3: Verified Registry

The verified registry is the distribution hub — the "npm" of the MCP ecosystem, but with security built in from day one rather than bolted on after a decade of incidents.

Package Signing with Sigstore

Unlike npm, which took years to implement package signing, MCPGuard uses Sigstore from day one. Every published MCP server package is:

  1. Signed by the publisher using Sigstore's keyless signing (OIDC identity from GitHub, Google, or Microsoft accounts)
  2. Counter-signed by MCPGuard after passing analysis (adding our attestation to the package)
  3. Logged to a transparency log (Rekor-compatible) so that any tampering is publicly detectable

The signature chain means consumers can verify: - Who published the package (identity) - That MCPGuard analyzed and approved it (attestation) - That the package has not been modified since signing (integrity) - The full history of signatures for audit (transparency)

Capability Attestation Protocol

This is MCPGuard's most novel contribution. Each MCP server in the registry includes a capability attestation document — a signed, machine-readable declaration of exactly what the server does:

{
  "attestation_version": "1.0",
  "server": "@company/mcp-database-tools",
  "version": "2.1.0",
  "capabilities": {
    "tools": [
      {
        "name": "query_database",
        "inputs": ["sql_query: string"],
        "outputs": ["rows: array"],
        "side_effects": ["database_read"],
        "network": ["postgres://*/5432"],
        "filesystem": "none"
      }
    ],
    "resources": ["database_schema"],
    "prompts": []
  },
  "permissions_required": {
    "network": ["postgres://*:5432"],
    "filesystem": {"read": [], "write": []},
    "process": "none",
    "environment": ["DATABASE_URL"]
  },
  "analysis_results": {
    "static_score": 92,
    "dynamic_score": 88,
    "trust_score": 87,
    "trust_tier": "verified",
    "last_analyzed": "2027-01-15T10:30:00Z"
  },
  "signatures": {
    "publisher": "sigstore://github.com/company",
    "mcpguard": "sigstore://mcpguard.dev/attestation/v1"
  }
}

The attestation is verified at install time and enforced at runtime. If a server attempts to access resources not declared in its attestation, the runtime monitor blocks the access and generates an alert.

Layer 4: Runtime Monitor

Static and dynamic analysis catch threats before deployment. Runtime monitoring catches threats that emerge after deployment — behavioral changes, compromised updates, and zero-day exploitation.

Monitoring Architecture

The runtime monitor operates as a lightweight sidecar or SDK hook that intercepts MCP protocol messages between the AI agent and the MCP server.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Agent as AI Agent<br/>(Claude/Cursor)
    participant Monitor as MCPGuard Monitor<br/>(Sidecar)
    participant Server as MCP Server
    participant Cloud as MCPGuard Cloud<br/>(Event Pipeline)

    Agent->>Monitor: tool/call (query_database)
    Monitor->>Monitor: Check against attestation
    Monitor->>Monitor: Log tool invocation
    Monitor->>Server: Forward tool/call
    Server->>Monitor: tool/result (rows)
    Monitor->>Monitor: Scan result for injection
    Monitor->>Monitor: Check behavioral baseline
    Monitor->>Agent: Forward tool/result
    Monitor-->>Cloud: Async: telemetry event

    Note over Monitor: If anomaly detected:
    Monitor->>Agent: BLOCK + alert
    Monitor-->>Cloud: Incident event

Behavioral Baseline Engine

When a monitored MCP server is first deployed, the monitor enters a "learning phase" (configurable, default 7 days) where it records baseline behavior:

  • Average tool invocations per minute
  • Typical result payload sizes
  • Network endpoints accessed
  • Filesystem paths accessed
  • Error rates and patterns
  • Resource consumption (CPU, memory)

After the learning phase, the monitor switches to "enforcement mode" where deviations from the baseline trigger alerts:

Deviation Threshold Response
New network endpoint Any new endpoint Alert + block (configurable)
Result payload 10x larger than baseline > 10x p95 Alert
Tool description changed at runtime Any change CRITICAL alert + auto-block
Filesystem access outside attestation Any violation Block + incident
Error rate spike > 3x baseline for 5 minutes Alert
CPU/memory spike > 5x baseline sustained Alert + throttle

Result Poisoning Detection

One of the most dangerous MCP attack vectors is result poisoning — an MCP server returns results that contain prompt injection payloads designed to manipulate the AI agent. The runtime monitor scans all tool results for:

  • Known prompt injection patterns (instruction override attempts)
  • Hidden Unicode characters used for steganographic injection
  • Base64-encoded payloads in text fields
  • Anomalous result structures that differ from the server's historical patterns
  • Results that reference tools or capabilities not present in the conversation

The detection engine uses a combination of regex pattern matching (fast, low false-positive for known patterns) and a small, fast LLM classifier (catches novel injection attempts at the cost of ~10ms latency per result).

Event Stream Architecture

All monitoring events flow through a Kafka-compatible event stream (we recommend Redpanda for operational simplicity) with the following topic structure:

  • mcpguard.events.tool-calls — Every tool invocation with timing and metadata
  • mcpguard.events.anomalies — Detected behavioral deviations
  • mcpguard.events.blocks — Enforcement actions taken
  • mcpguard.events.attestation-violations — Capability attestation breaches
  • mcpguard.events.result-scans — Result poisoning detection events

Enterprise customers can consume these streams directly for integration with their SIEM (Splunk, Sentinel, Elastic Security) or SOAR platforms.

Layer 5: Incident Dashboard

The incident dashboard is the human interface for security teams. It transforms raw monitoring events into actionable intelligence.

Dashboard Components

Real-Time Event Feed. A live-updating stream of security events across all monitored MCP servers. Filterable by severity, server, event type, and time range. Each event links to the underlying telemetry data for investigation.

Server Health Grid. A bird's-eye view of all MCP servers in the organization's environment. Each server is represented as a tile colored by its current health status (green/yellow/orange/red). Clicking a tile drills into that server's detailed behavioral profile.

Incident Timeline. When an incident is detected, the dashboard automatically constructs a timeline from the event stream:

  1. First anomalous event (with timestamp and context)
  2. Escalation events (if the anomaly persisted or worsened)
  3. Enforcement actions taken (blocks, quarantines)
  4. Affected users and sessions
  5. Recommended remediation steps

Trust Score Trends. Historical charts showing how trust scores for each server have changed over time. This makes it easy to spot the gradual degradation that indicates a supply chain compromise (the "slow burn" attack pattern).

Policy Compliance. For enterprises with defined trust policies (e.g., "only Verified-tier servers in production"), the dashboard shows compliance status with drill-down into violations.

Alert Pipeline

Alerts flow through a configurable pipeline:

  1. Detection — Runtime monitor or scheduled re-scan identifies an issue
  2. Deduplication — Multiple alerts for the same root cause are grouped
  3. Enrichment — Alert is enriched with server metadata, trust score, affected users
  4. Routing — Alert routes to the appropriate channel based on severity and server owner
  5. Escalation — If not acknowledged within SLA, alert escalates to next tier

Integration targets: PagerDuty, OpsGenie, Slack, Microsoft Teams, email, webhook.

Security of the Platform Itself

A security platform must be secure. MCPGuard's own security posture:

  • Zero-trust architecture — Every internal service authenticates via mTLS
  • Secrets in HSM — Signing keys stored in AWS CloudHSM, never in environment variables
  • Immutable audit trail — All administrative actions logged to append-only storage
  • Pen-tested quarterly — Third-party penetration testing of all public-facing surfaces
  • SOC 2 Type II — Compliance from Year 1 (requirement for enterprise sales)
  • Bug bounty program — Launching at public beta to incentivize external security research

Technical Risks and Mitigations

Risk Likelihood Impact Mitigation
MCP protocol changes break scanner High Medium Modular parser architecture, active participation in MCP spec development
Sophisticated evasion bypasses analysis Medium High Layered detection (static + dynamic + runtime), continuous red-teaming
False positives erode publisher trust Medium High Human review queue for edge cases, publisher appeal process
Scanner itself becomes attack target Low Critical Isolated VM execution, no host access from sandbox, regular pen testing
Alternative MCP registries fragment ecosystem Medium Medium Open API, free tier, partnership with major AI platforms
Cost of dynamic analysis at scale Medium Medium Optimized VM pool, skip full sandbox for minor version updates

Conclusion

MCPGuard's technical architecture is designed around one principle: defense in depth. No single layer is sufficient. Static analysis catches known patterns. Dynamic analysis catches behavioral threats. Runtime monitoring catches post-deployment changes. The trust score engine synthesizes all signals into an actionable decision. And the incident dashboard gives security teams the visibility they need to respond.

The architecture is deliberately modular. We can ship the static scanner and registry (Phase 1) with a small team in four months, then iterate toward runtime monitoring and enterprise features based on customer feedback. Each layer adds value independently while becoming more powerful in combination.

For the MCP ecosystem to achieve enterprise adoption, it needs a security infrastructure layer. MCPGuard is that layer. The next chapter maps this architecture to the market opportunity and go-to-market strategy that turns the technology into a business.

Chapter 12: MCPGuard Market & Go-to-Market

The Market No One Has Captured Yet

Model Context Protocol has done something remarkable: it created a universal plugin system for AI agents in less than 18 months. By mid-2026, MCP servers are the default mechanism for extending AI assistants with external capabilities — database queries, API integrations, file system tools, cloud infrastructure management. Anthropic's Claude, Cursor, Windsurf, and dozens of custom enterprise agents all speak MCP.

But the ecosystem grew faster than its security infrastructure. There are over 10,000 MCP servers available today across GitHub, npm, and various community directories. By 2027, conservative estimates project 100,000+. There is no centralized security scanning, no trusted registry, no runtime monitoring, and no incident response capability for this ecosystem.

MCPGuard is positioned to be the security layer for this ecosystem. This chapter quantifies the market opportunity, defines the go-to-market strategy, and presents the financial model that makes this a compelling venture investment.

Competitive Moat

MCPGuard's moat deepens over time through four mechanisms:

1. Threat Intelligence Network Effect. Every MCP server scanned adds to our threat intelligence database. The more servers we analyze, the better our pattern detection becomes. A competitor starting in 2028 would need to analyze the entire backlog of 100,000+ servers to match our baseline — a multi-year effort.

2. Publisher Ecosystem Lock-in. Once publishers sign their packages through MCPGuard and build their reputation on our trust score system, switching costs are high. Their trust history, verified identity, and accumulated reputation do not transfer to a competitor.

3. Enterprise Policy Integration. When enterprises define trust policies in MCPGuard (e.g., "only Verified-tier servers in production"), these policies reference our trust score system. Switching requires re-evaluating every server against a new scoring system — a non-trivial effort for organizations with hundreds of MCP integrations.

4. Specification Influence. By participating actively in MCP specification development and contributing security extensions (capability attestation, signing standards), we embed MCPGuard's approach into the protocol itself. This is the playbook that Let's Encrypt used to become the default TLS certificate authority.

Pricing Strategy

Freemium Model

MCPGuard uses a freemium model designed to maximize developer adoption (free tier) while capturing enterprise revenue (paid tiers). This follows the proven playbook of Snyk, Socket.dev, and GitHub Security.

Tier Price Target Includes
Community Free Individual developers CLI scanner, 50 scans/month, basic trust scores, public registry access

Pricing Rationale

Why per-developer? MCP security risk scales with the number of developers using AI agents, not with the number of servers (one server can be used by many developers). Per-developer pricing is also the standard model in DevSecOps tools, making procurement familiar for enterprise buyers.

Why not per-server? We considered per-server pricing but rejected it because: 1. It penalizes organizations for having diverse tool integrations (bad incentive) 2. Server count fluctuates as teams experiment, making budgeting unpredictable 3. Enterprise procurement teams prefer per-seat models they can map to headcount

Free tier economics: At 50 scans/month, the marginal cost per free user is approximately $0.15/month (compute + storage). We budget for 100,000 free users at $15K/month — well within marketing spend for the leads generated.

Distribution Strategy

Channel 1: Developer Community (Awareness + Free Adoption)

Open-source CLI tool. The mcpguard CLI scanner is open source (Apache 2.0). Developers can npm install -g mcpguard and immediately scan any MCP server. This creates the initial adoption wedge.

npm/GitHub integration. We publish MCPGuard scan results as GitHub Actions annotations and npm advisory notices. When developers install an MCP server via npm, they see MCPGuard's trust score in the output (via npm hooks integration).

Content marketing. We publish weekly "MCP Security Digest" featuring: - Newly discovered vulnerabilities in popular MCP servers - Trust score changes for trending servers - Best practices for MCP server publishers - Technical deep dives on attack techniques

This positions MCPGuard as the authoritative voice in MCP security — the same playbook that Snyk used to dominate JavaScript security mindshare.

Conference presence. Talks at AI engineering conferences (AI Engineer Summit, NeurIPS workshops), security conferences (DEF CON AI Village, BSides), and developer conferences (KubeCon, ReactConf). Topic: "The MCP Supply Chain Problem You Don't Know You Have."

VS Code Extension. A VS Code extension that shows MCPGuard trust scores inline when configuring MCP servers. Cursor Integration. Cursor is the fastest-growing AI coding tool and a heavy MCP user. A Cursor plugin that integrates MCPGuard scanning into Cursor's MCP server management UI would capture the highest-value developer segment.

JetBrains Plugin. For enterprise Java/Kotlin developers using AI assistants within JetBrains IDEs.

Sales motion: 1. Inbound from developer adoption. Developer installs free CLI → scans find issues → shares results with security team → security team evaluates enterprise tier. This is the product-led growth (PLG) motion. 2. Outbound to security teams. Direct outreach to CISOs at organizations with known AI agent deployments. Lead with: "Your developers are installing unvetted MCP servers. Here's what we found in your environment." 3. Channel partnerships. Partner with managed security service providers (MSSPs) and AI consulting firms who are deploying MCP-based solutions for clients.

Enterprise sales cycle: 45-90 days (shorter than typical security tools because the threat is immediate and the product is self-service to try).

Channel 4: Platform Partnerships (Scale)

Anthropic partnership. MCPGuard as the recommended security layer for the MCP ecosystem. Potential integration into Claude's MCP server management workflow. This is the highest-leverage partnership — Anthropic has strong incentives to ensure MCP ecosystem security.

Cloud marketplace. AWS Marketplace, Azure Marketplace, GCP Marketplace listings for enterprise procurement. Marketplace listings reduce procurement friction (use existing cloud commit, no new vendor PO needed).

AI platform integrations. Direct integration with AI agent orchestration platforms (LangChain, CrewAI, AutoGPT) that use MCP for tool integration. These platforms can bundle MCPGuard scanning as a built-in feature.

Chapter 14: The Problem — AI Agents Store Secrets in Plaintext

The Credential Crisis Hiding in Every Developer's Home Directory

Every AI coding agent on the market today has the same dirty secret: they store credentials insecurely. OAuth tokens in plaintext JSON files. API keys in unencrypted conversation history. Passwords pasted into sessions that persist on disk indefinitely. Tokens in environment variables that never expire or rotate.

This is not speculation. This is what we found when we performed a deep security audit of a production AI coding agent — one of the most widely deployed, from one of the most security-conscious companies in the industry. The audit uncovered 50 vulnerabilities organized into 7 dependency chains. The credential storage chain alone contained 8 HIGH-severity findings, each individually sufficient to compromise every secret a developer has shared with or through the agent.

This chapter presents the specific vulnerabilities we found, explains why they exist, quantifies the enterprise-wide exposure, and makes the case that credential management for AI agents is not a feature request — it is an urgent infrastructure gap that represents a venture-scale opportunity.

What We Found: 8 HIGH-Severity Credential Vulnerabilities

Our audit targeted a production AI coding agent: a 500,000+ line TypeScript/Node.js codebase that runs on developer machines, manages OAuth authentication, stores conversation history, and connects to cloud APIs via bridge servers and WebSocket connections. The agent runs on macOS, Linux, and Windows. Millions of developers use it daily.

Here are the credential storage vulnerabilities we discovered, ordered by CVSS severity score.

Finding 1: Plaintext Credential Storage on Non-macOS Platforms

Severity: HIGH | CVSS: 7.1 | CWE: CWE-256 (Plaintext Storage of a Password)

Location: utils/secureStorage/index.ts:9

The function getSecureStorage() returns different storage backends depending on the operating system. On macOS, it uses the system keychain. On every other platform — Linux, Windows, WSL — it returns plainTextStorage, which writes OAuth tokens and credentials as a JSON file at ~/.claude/.credentials.json with chmod 0600 permissions.

The source code contained a telling comment:

// TODO: add libsecret support for Linux
return plainTextStorage

A TODO comment guarding the credential storage path for every non-macOS user. Every Linux developer, every WSL user, every CI/CD pipeline, every container — all using plaintext credential storage protected by nothing more than file permissions.

Why this matters: chmod 0600 prevents other users on the same system from reading the file. It does not prevent: - Root access (standard in containers, common in cloud instances) - Same-user process access (any malware running as the developer) - Backup exfiltration (Time Machine, cloud sync, corporate backup agents) - Disk imaging (forensic tools, VM snapshots) - Container volume mounts (shared filesystems in Docker/Kubernetes)

Exploitation scenario: A developer runs the AI agent in a Docker container (a common setup for isolated development environments). The container stores OAuth tokens in ~/.claude/.credentials.json inside the container's writable layer. Another process in the same container — or anything with access to the Docker socket — reads the credentials file and exfiltrates the tokens.

Finding 2: Plaintext Credential Fallback Storage

Severity: HIGH | CVSS: 7.1 | CWE: CWE-312 (Cleartext Storage of Sensitive Information)

Location: utils/secureStorage/plainTextStorage.ts:57

Even on macOS where the keychain is the primary storage, a fallback mechanism silently activates when keychain operations fail. This fallback writes credentials to the same plaintext JSON file.

The data flow:

OAuth token obtained
  → saveOAuthTokensIfNeeded()
    → secureStorage.write()
      → macOS keychain write attempt
        → FAILS (Docker container, SSH session, CI runner)
          → fallbackStorage activates silently
            → plainTextStorage.write()
              → .credentials.json on disk in plaintext

The critical issue is the word "silently." The fallback logs a warning at debug level, but the user is never informed that their credentials just fell from keychain-level security to plaintext-on-disk. No confirmation prompt. No visible warning. Just a debug log line that 99.9% of users will never see.

Why this matters: macOS developers who believe their credentials are protected by the system keychain may actually be using plaintext storage without knowing it. Common scenarios that trigger the fallback: - Running in a Docker container (no keychain available) - SSH session without a GUI (keychain requires user interaction) - CI/CD pipeline (headless environment) - Freshly provisioned cloud instance (keychain not configured) - macOS keychain locked after restart (user has not unlocked it)

Finding 3: Conversation History Stored in Plaintext

Severity: HIGH | CVSS: 7.0 | CWE: CWE-312 (Cleartext Storage of Sensitive Information)

Location: history.ts:115

Every conversation with the AI agent is stored in a plaintext JSONL file at ~/.claude/history.jsonl. Content pasted into sessions under 1,024 characters is stored inline in the history entry. Larger pastes are stored in individual plaintext files at ~/.claude/paste-cache/{sha256-hash}.txt.

There is no encryption. There is no TTL. There is no automatic purging. There is no secret detection or redaction.

This means that when a developer pastes an API key into a session — a common action when configuring cloud services, debugging authentication issues, or setting up environment variables — that API key persists on disk indefinitely in cleartext. The full data flow:

Developer pastes API key into session
  → LogEntry created with pastedContents field
    → writeToFile() appends to history.jsonl (plaintext)
    → If paste > 1024 chars: paste-cache/{sha256}.txt (plaintext)
      → File persists until manual deletion
        → Backup software captures file
          → Cloud sync uploads to storage
            → API key now in 3+ locations, all plaintext

Why this matters: Developers routinely share secrets with AI agents: - "Here's my AWS access key, help me configure the SDK" - "This is the database connection string, why am I getting a connection error?" - "My JWT token is [token], decode it and tell me what scopes are missing" - Copy-pasting .env file contents for debugging

Each of these interactions creates a permanent plaintext record. Over time, a developer's history file becomes a comprehensive inventory of every secret they have ever shared with the agent.

Finding 4: Plaintext Credential Storage on Linux

Severity: HIGH | CVSS: 6.5 | CWE: CWE-922 (Insecure Storage of Sensitive Information)

Location: utils/secureStorage/index.ts:16

This is the Linux-specific manifestation of Finding 1, distinguished because Linux is the primary operating system for cloud development, CI/CD pipelines, and containerized workloads — environments where credential security is most critical.

On macOS, the keychain provides hardware-backed credential storage through the Secure Enclave. On Linux, equivalent functionality exists through libsecret (GNOME Keyring, KDE Wallet) and the D-Bus Secret Service API. None of these are implemented. The code simply returns plainTextStorage.

Enterprise exposure: According to the Stack Overflow 2025 Developer Survey, 48% of professional developers use Linux as their primary development OS. For cloud-native development and DevOps, the number is higher — approximately 72% by industry estimates. Every one of these developers using this AI agent stores credentials in plaintext.

Finding 5: Environment Variable Tokens Never Expire

Severity: HIGH (by impact, MEDIUM by CVSS) | CVSS: 6.5 | CWE: CWE-613 (Insufficient Session Expiration)

Location: utils/auth.ts:1260

Tokens provided via the CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN environment variable are assigned expiresAt: null and refreshToken: null. The client treats them as immortal — they never expire, never refresh, and never rotate.

// Reconstructed from audit findings
{
  accessToken: process.env.CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN,
  refreshToken: null,    // No refresh mechanism
  expiresAt: null,       // No expiry check
}

The isTokenExpired() function returns false for null expiry. The checkAndRefreshOAuthTokenIfNeeded() function skips refresh for tokens without a refresh token. The result: a leaked environment variable token remains usable from the client's perspective indefinitely, even after server-side revocation, because the client never checks.

Why this matters: CI/CD pipelines are the primary consumers of environment variable tokens. A token leaked from a CI pipeline (through log exposure, configuration drift, or compromised runner) can be used by an attacker until someone manually discovers and revokes it. The client provides no early warning.

Findings 6-8: The Supporting Chain

Beyond the five primary findings above, three additional HIGH-severity credential issues complete the chain:

Finding 6: JWT Tokens Decoded Without Signature Verification (CVSS 7.5, CWE-347)

The bridge client's decodeJwtPayload() function performs base64 decoding of JWT payloads without verifying the signature. An attacker who can intercept the connection (corporate proxy, compromised DNS) can forge JWTs with manipulated expiry claims, preventing token refresh and keeping revoked tokens active indefinitely.

Finding 7: Proxy Credentials in WebSocket Headers (CVSS 5.4, CWE-522)

When connecting through corporate proxies, proxy authentication credentials are sent in WebSocket upgrade headers and encoded as Base64 Basic Auth in memory. These credentials remain on the heap after use without zeroing.

Finding 8: TOCTOU Race in Credential File Write (CVSS 4.7, CWE-367)

The plaintext credential storage writes credentials using a non-atomic write pattern: open file, write content, set permissions. Between the write and chmod, a brief window exists where the file may be readable by other users.

The Systemic Problem: Why Every AI Agent Is Vulnerable

The eight findings above are from one agent. But the underlying problem is systemic — every AI coding agent faces the same credential management challenges, and most solve them the same way (or worse).

Why Agents Handle Credentials Poorly

1. Credential management is not the core product. AI coding agents are built by AI/ML teams optimized for model performance, code generation quality, and developer experience. Secure credential storage is a solved problem in theory (OS keychains, secret managers) but a complex engineering challenge in practice. It falls into the "we'll get to it" category — hence the TODO comment in the source code.

2. Cross-platform complexity. A credential storage solution that works on macOS, Linux, Windows, WSL, Docker, CI/CD runners, and cloud instances requires platform-specific integrations (keychain, libsecret, DPAPI, credential manager) plus fallback paths for environments where none are available. Most teams implement the macOS path (loudest user base) and punt on the rest.

3. The conversation history problem is new. Traditional CLI tools do not store conversation history. AI agents do — because conversations are the core interface. But conversation history is also the most dangerous data surface, because developers routinely share secrets during conversations. Existing secret scanning tools (gitleaks, truffleHog) scan git repositories, not conversation history files.

4. Token lifecycle management adds operational complexity. Short-lived tokens with automatic rotation require server-side coordination, refresh token storage, expiry monitoring, and graceful degradation when refresh fails. Environment variable tokens are simpler — but simpler means insecure, because simplicity comes at the cost of never expiring.

Real-World Attack Chains

Our research identified three high-impact attack chains that combine multiple vulnerabilities:

Chain 1: Backup Exfiltration

Developer authenticates with AI agent
  → OAuth token stored in ~/.agent/.credentials.json (plaintext)
  → Time Machine backs up home directory hourly
  → Backup stored on NAS accessible to IT staff
  → IT staff member (or compromised NAS) reads backup
  → OAuth token extracted from backup
  → Attacker accesses developer's AI API account

Chain 2: Container Escape

Developer runs AI agent in Docker container for isolation
  → Keychain unavailable in container (fallback activates silently)
  → Credentials stored plaintext in container writable layer
  → Docker socket exposed for CI/CD management
  → Malicious CI job reads container filesystem
  → Credentials exfiltrated via container inspection

Chain 3: Conversation History Mining

Developer pastes AWS key into AI agent chat session
  → Secret stored in history.jsonl indefinitely (no TTL, no redaction)
  → Developer leaves company; laptop returned to IT
  → IT re-images laptop but does not securely wipe
  → Next employee receives laptop
  → Previous developer's secrets accessible in hidden directories

Each chain is individually plausible and collectively represents the kind of risk that keeps CISOs awake at night — diffuse, hard to detect, and impossible to remediate with current tools.

The Compliance Time Bomb

The credential storage problem is not just a security risk — it is a compliance violation waiting to be discovered.

Regulatory Frameworks at Risk

SOC 2 Type II. The Trust Services Criteria require that "the entity authorizes, modifies, or removes access to data, software, functions, and other protected information assets based on roles" (CC6.1) and that "confidential information is protected during the processes of storing, using, transmitting, and disposing" (C1.2). Plaintext credential storage on developer machines violates both criteria.

PCI DSS 4.0. Requirement 3.5 mandates that primary account numbers (PANs) and sensitive authentication data are rendered unreadable anywhere they are stored. Developers who paste payment API keys into AI agents create PCI scope on every machine with unencrypted conversation history.

GDPR. Article 32 requires "encryption of personal data" as a technical measure. If AI agents process personal data (common in development and debugging), the plaintext conversation history creates a GDPR violation in every EU-based development environment.

HIPAA. The Security Rule requires encryption of electronic protected health information (ePHI) at rest. Healthcare developers using AI agents to work with ePHI systems create a HIPAA violation every time they paste patient-related data into a session.

NIST 800-53. Control SC-28 (Protection of Information at Rest) requires encryption of sensitive data. Federal contractors using AI agents with plaintext credential storage are out of compliance.

The Audit Scenario

Imagine a compliance auditor asks: "Show me how your developers' AI coding tools store credentials."

The honest answer for most organizations today: "We don't know. Each tool stores credentials in its own format, in hidden directories on developer machines. We have no visibility, no encryption, and no policy enforcement."

This answer fails every framework listed above. And as AI tool adoption grows, auditors are beginning to ask this question.

The Enterprise Blocker

The credential problem is not just creating risk — it is actively blocking enterprise AI adoption.

CISOs Are Saying No

In conversations with enterprise security teams, we hear the same concerns repeatedly:

"We cannot deploy AI coding tools on machines with access to production credentials." This means developers must use AI tools on isolated machines or VMs without access to the systems they need to work on — defeating the purpose of AI-assisted development.

"Our DLP tools flag AI agent configuration files as credential leaks." Data Loss Prevention tools detect plaintext tokens in AI agent directories and generate alerts. Security teams then spend time investigating false-alarm-like findings that are actually real credential exposures, but ones they cannot fix because the agent provides no alternative storage mechanism.

"We need an audit trail for every credential access by every AI tool." Compliance requirements demand that organizations know which credentials are being accessed, by which tools, at what time, for what purpose. AI agents provide none of this visibility.

"We blocked [Agent X] after finding OAuth tokens in plaintext during a pen test." Real incident from a Fortune 500 financial services company. Their penetration test found plaintext OAuth tokens in the AI agent's configuration directory. The agent was banned from all corporate machines pending a fix. That fix has not come — because the agent vendor does not offer encrypted credential storage.

Why This Is a Startup, Not a Feature

A reasonable question: why will AI agent vendors not solve this themselves? The answer is nuanced.

Some will — partially. Major AI tool vendors will eventually implement OS keychain integration across platforms. The macOS path will come first (it always does). Linux libsecret support will follow. This addresses Findings 1, 2, and 4 from our audit — the plaintext storage findings.

But the systemic problems will remain:

  1. Conversation history secret detection requires a specialized scanning engine that understands credential patterns across hundreds of secret types. Building and maintaining this is a full product, not a feature.

  2. Cross-tool credential management cannot be solved by any single vendor. Each vendor can secure their own storage, but the proliferation problem (3,750 credential files per enterprise) requires a layer that sits above individual tools.

  3. Audit trails and compliance reporting require a centralized system that tracks credential access across all AI tools, maps to compliance frameworks, and generates reports. No individual AI tool vendor has the incentive or capability to build this for their competitors' products.

  4. Token lifecycle management (rotation, expiry enforcement, revocation propagation) requires coordination between the agent, the secret storage layer, and the credential provider. This is middleware, not a feature.

  5. Enterprise policy enforcement (which tools can access which credentials, in which environments, under what conditions) requires a policy engine that spans the entire AI tool ecosystem.

The credential management problem for AI agents is the same class of problem that HashiCorp Vault solved for cloud infrastructure: too complex for any single application to solve well, too critical for enterprises to ignore, and too cross-cutting for any single vendor to own.

Capability 1: Encrypted Vault

The encrypted vault replaces every AI agent's insecure credential storage with a single, encrypted, OS-integrated credential store.

What it does: - Intercepts credential write operations from AI agents (OAuth tokens, API keys, session tokens) - Encrypts credentials using XSalsa20-Poly1305 (libsodium) before writing to disk - Integrates with OS keychain for key management (macOS Keychain, Linux libsecret/GNOME Keyring, Windows DPAPI/Credential Manager) - Provides a unified credential access API that all AI agents use instead of their own storage

What it replaces: - ~/.claude/.credentials.json (plaintext JSON) - ~/.cursor/auth.json (plaintext JSON) - ~/.copilot/hosts.json (plaintext JSON) - Every other AI agent's ad-hoc credential file

Key design decision: VaultAgent does not require agents to be modified. The Agent SDK hooks into each agent's credential storage path via filesystem-level interception (on macOS: Endpoint Security framework; on Linux: eBPF/fanotify; on Windows: minifilter driver). When an agent writes to its credential file, VaultAgent transparently encrypts the content. When the agent reads, VaultAgent transparently decrypts. From the agent's perspective, nothing changes. From a security perspective, everything changes.

Encryption at rest:

Agent writes: {"accessToken": "sk-ant-....", "refreshToken": "rt-..."}
  → VaultAgent intercepts write
    → Generate per-file nonce (24 bytes, random)
    → Encrypt payload: XSalsa20-Poly1305(payload, key, nonce)
    → Key derived from: OS keychain master key + machine-specific salt
    → Write encrypted blob + nonce to original file path
    → Agent sees success (transparent)

Agent reads: (encrypted blob on disk)
  → VaultAgent intercepts read
    → Retrieve key from OS keychain
    → Decrypt: XSalsa20-Poly1305_open(blob, key, nonce)
    → Return plaintext to agent
    → Agent sees normal JSON (transparent)

Capability 2: Secret Scanner

The secret scanner monitors AI agent conversation histories, tool outputs, and telemetry for secrets that should not be stored in plaintext.

What it scans: - Conversation history files (JSONL, SQLite, custom formats) - Paste cache directories - Agent configuration files - Debug log files - Telemetry metadata

What it detects:

Secret Type Detection Method Examples
AWS access keys Regex: AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16} AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE
GitHub tokens Regex: gh[pso]_[a-zA-Z0-9]{36,} ghp_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
API keys (generic) High-entropy string detection + context sk-proj-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
Database connection strings URI pattern matching postgres://user:pass@host:5432/db
Private keys PEM header/footer detection -----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----
JWT tokens Three-part base64 pattern eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIs...
OAuth tokens Prefix matching + entropy ya29.a0AfH6SMBxxxxxxxxx
Passwords in context NLP-based contextual detection "password is hunter2"
SSH keys Key format detection ssh-rsa AAAA...
Certificate files PEM/DER pattern detection -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----

Actions on detection:

The scanner operates in three modes, configurable per environment:

  1. Detect mode (default for evaluation): Identifies secrets and generates alerts without modifying files. Reports to the admin dashboard with severity, location, and remediation guidance.

  2. Redact mode (recommended for production): Automatically redacts detected secrets in conversation history and logs, replacing them with references: [REDACTED: AWS_ACCESS_KEY detected, ref: VA-2027-001]. The original secret is moved to the encrypted vault with a cross-reference.

  3. Block mode (available for high-security environments): Prevents secrets from being written to unencrypted storage in the first place. When an agent attempts to write a file containing a detected secret, VaultAgent intercepts the write and stores the secret in the vault, replacing it with a reference in the file.

Scanner performance: The scanner operates as a background daemon, processing file changes via filesystem event notifications (FSEvents on macOS, inotify on Linux, ReadDirectoryChangesW on Windows). Typical latency: <100ms from file write to detection. CPU overhead: <2% on a modern development machine.

Capability 3: Lifecycle Manager

The lifecycle manager solves the "immortal token" problem identified in our audit research. It manages the complete lifecycle of credentials used by AI agents: creation, rotation, expiry enforcement, and revocation.

Token rotation: - Monitors credential expiry timestamps across all managed agents - Proactively refreshes tokens before expiry (configurable buffer, default: 10% of token lifetime) - For tokens without refresh mechanisms (environment variable tokens), enforces a maximum lifetime (configurable, default: 24 hours) and alerts when tokens should be rotated - Maintains rotation history for audit trail

Expiry enforcement: - Overrides the "immortal token" pattern where agents set expiresAt: null - Applies organization-defined maximum token lifetimes - Alerts when tokens exceed maximum age - Supports graceful degradation: warn → restrict → revoke pipeline

Revocation propagation: - When a credential is revoked (server-side or admin-initiated), VaultAgent removes it from all agent credential stores simultaneously - Revocation is immediate and atomic — no agent continues using a revoked credential - Revocation events are logged with full context (who revoked, why, which agents affected)

Environment variable token management: - Monitors *_TOKEN, *_KEY, *_SECRET, *_PASSWORD environment variables - Replaces long-lived env var tokens with short-lived tokens from VaultAgent - Provides a CLI tool: vaultagent inject that sets environment variables from the encrypted vault with automatic expiry - Integrates with CI/CD systems (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins) for pipeline token management

Capability 5: Zero-Knowledge Architecture

The most critical design decision in VaultAgent is what it does NOT know.

VaultAgent never sees plaintext credentials on our servers. All encryption and decryption happens locally on the developer's machine. The encryption key is derived from the OS keychain and never leaves the device. Our cloud backend stores only:

  • Encrypted credential metadata (what type, when created, when last accessed)
  • Policy configurations
  • Audit log entries (with credential IDs, not credential values)
  • License and usage telemetry

Why zero-knowledge matters:

  1. Trust model. If VaultAgent could read your credentials, you would need to trust us not to be compromised. With zero-knowledge, a breach of our servers exposes no credential data.

  2. Compliance simplification. VaultAgent's cloud backend is not in scope for PCI, HIPAA, or other credential-focused compliance frameworks because it never processes credentials.

  3. Enterprise procurement. Security teams evaluating VaultAgent can verify the zero-knowledge claim through code audit (we publish the encryption module as open source) and network traffic analysis (no plaintext credentials leave the machine).

Windsurf ~/.windsurf/credentials.json Filesystem interception Transparent
Continue.dev ~/.continue/auth.json Filesystem interception Transparent
Custom agents Configurable paths Filesystem interception + SDK SDK integration (optional)

Transparent mode requires zero changes to the AI agent. VaultAgent watches the known credential file paths and intercepts reads/writes at the filesystem level. This is the primary integration path for existing agents.

SDK mode provides deeper integration for agents that want to use VaultAgent's API directly:

import { VaultAgent } from '@vaultagent/sdk';

const vault = new VaultAgent({
  appName: 'my-custom-agent',
  encryptionLevel: 'hardware', // Use OS keychain
});

// Store a credential
await vault.store({
  key: 'anthropic-oauth',
  value: accessToken,
  type: 'oauth_token',
  expiresAt: new Date(Date.now() + 3600_000),
  metadata: { provider: 'anthropic', scope: 'write' },
});

// Retrieve a credential
const token = await vault.retrieve('anthropic-oauth');

// Credential is automatically rotated before expiry
// Credential access is automatically logged
// Credential is automatically encrypted at rest

Technical Differentiators: What Makes VaultAgent Hard to Replicate

Five technical capabilities that create defensibility beyond market timing:

1. Cross-Agent Behavioral Fingerprinting. VaultAgent builds a behavioral model of how each AI agent accesses credentials. This fingerprint enables anomaly detection: if a process claiming to be Claude Code accesses credentials using a pattern that does not match Claude Code's known behavior, VaultAgent blocks the access. Building this fingerprint library requires observing millions of credential access events across thousands of deployments — a dataset that grows with our customer base.

2. Secret Pattern Database. Our scanner maintains a curated database of 400+ secret patterns with context-specific tuning. This database is continuously updated as new AI tools emerge and new secret formats appear. The database is the product of ongoing security research, not a one-time engineering effort. Competitors can replicate the initial patterns, but staying current requires the same research investment.

3. Platform-Specific Encryption Integrations. Deep integration with macOS Keychain, Linux libsecret, Windows DPAPI, and hardware security modules (TPM, Secure Enclave) across all major platforms. Each integration is a multi-week engineering effort with platform-specific edge cases. The combined matrix (3 platforms x 2+ security backends per platform) represents 6+ months of platform engineering that any competitor must replicate.

4. Agent Adapter Library. Transparent filesystem interception for 6+ AI agents, each with its own credential file format, storage location, and access pattern. Each adapter requires reverse-engineering the agent's credential storage behavior. As new agents launch, we add adapters within days — competitors starting from zero face a growing backlog.

5. Compliance Template Library. Pre-built compliance report templates mapped to SOC 2, PCI DSS, HIPAA, GDPR, and NIST 800-53. Each template was developed with input from compliance auditors to ensure it meets the specific evidence requirements of each framework. Creating audit-ready templates requires compliance expertise, not just engineering.

The next chapter details the technical architecture that makes all of this work.

Chapter 16: VaultAgent Technical Architecture

Engineering the Trust Layer for AI Agent Credentials

This chapter is the engineering blueprint for VaultAgent. Every component described here maps to a system that must be built, deployed, and maintained at scale. We cover the five core subsystems in implementation detail: the Agent SDK, the encrypted vault, the secret scanner, the lifecycle manager, and the audit dashboard. We also address the cross-cutting concerns that determine whether the system works in practice: performance, reliability, platform compatibility, and the security of VaultAgent itself.

The architecture follows two non-negotiable constraints:

  1. Zero-knowledge. VaultAgent's cloud infrastructure never sees plaintext credentials. All encryption and decryption happens on the developer's machine. This is not a nice-to-have — it is the architectural foundation that makes enterprise adoption possible.

  2. Transparent integration. Existing AI coding agents must work with VaultAgent without modification. Developers should not need to change their workflow. The security layer must be invisible during normal operation and visible only when it prevents a problem.

Component 1: Agent SDK Layer

The Agent SDK is the interface between AI coding agents and VaultAgent's security services. It provides three integration methods, ordered from least to most invasive.

Filesystem Hooks (Primary — Zero-Config)

The filesystem hook intercepts file I/O operations on known credential file paths. This requires no changes to any AI agent — VaultAgent watches the filesystem and transparently encrypts/decrypts credential files.

macOS Implementation: Endpoint Security Framework (ESF)

macOS provides the Endpoint Security framework for monitoring filesystem events. VaultAgent registers as an ESF client and subscribes to ES_EVENT_TYPE_NOTIFY_WRITE and ES_EVENT_TYPE_AUTH_OPEN events on monitored paths.

Event flow:
1. Claude Code calls writeFileSync("~/.claude/.credentials.json", data)
2. ESF delivers ES_EVENT_TYPE_NOTIFY_WRITE to VaultAgent
3. VaultAgent reads the written file
4. VaultAgent encrypts the content: encrypt(data, key, nonce)
5. VaultAgent writes encrypted blob back to the same path
6. Latency added: ~5ms (encryption) + ~2ms (write)

Read flow:
1. Claude Code calls readFileSync("~/.claude/.credentials.json")
2. ESF delivers ES_EVENT_TYPE_AUTH_OPEN to VaultAgent
3. VaultAgent decrypts file content to a tmpfs-backed temporary file
4. VaultAgent redirects the read to the decrypted temporary
5. Temporary file is zeroed and deleted after read completes
6. Latency added: ~5ms (decryption) + ~1ms (tmpfs)

ESF requires a system extension (kext-free since macOS 10.15.4) distributed via MDM or user-approved installation. This is the same mechanism used by security products like CrowdStrike Falcon and SentinelOne.

Linux Implementation: eBPF + fanotify

On Linux, VaultAgent uses a combination of fanotify (for filesystem event monitoring) and eBPF (for high-performance path filtering).

fanotify provides:
- FAN_CLOSE_WRITE: notification when a file is written and closed
- FAN_OPEN_PERM: permission event before file open (allows blocking)

eBPF provides:
- High-performance path filtering (avoid processing irrelevant filesystem events)
- Process identification (know which agent is accessing which credential)
- Zero-copy event processing (minimal overhead)

The Linux implementation requires CAP_SYS_ADMIN for fanotify and CAP_BPF for eBPF program loading. VaultAgent runs as a systemd service with these capabilities.

Windows Implementation: Minifilter Driver

On Windows, VaultAgent uses a minifilter driver to intercept file I/O on credential paths. The minifilter is a signed, Microsoft-approved driver (WHQL certified for enterprise deployment).

Component 2: Encrypted Vault

The encrypted vault is the core storage engine. It replaces every agent's insecure credential file with an encrypted blob that can only be decrypted on the same machine, by the same user, with the OS keychain available.

Encryption Architecture

graph TB
    subgraph "Key Hierarchy"
        MASTER[Master Key<br/>Stored in OS Keychain<br/>256-bit random]
        DERIVE[Key Derivation<br/>Argon2id + machine salt]
        FILE_KEY[Per-File Key<br/>Derived from master + file ID]
    end

    subgraph "Encryption"
        PLAIN[Plaintext Credential<br/>JSON payload]
        NONCE[Random Nonce<br/>24 bytes per encryption]
        ENCRYPT[XSalsa20-Poly1305<br/>libsodium crypto_secretbox]
        BLOB[Encrypted Blob<br/>nonce || ciphertext || tag]
    end

    subgraph "Storage"
        DISK[Disk Storage<br/>~/.vaultagent/vault/{id}.enc]
        META[Metadata<br/>~/.vaultagent/meta.db (SQLite)]
    end

    MASTER --> DERIVE
    DERIVE --> FILE_KEY
    FILE_KEY --> ENCRYPT
    PLAIN --> ENCRYPT
    NONCE --> ENCRYPT
    ENCRYPT --> BLOB
    BLOB --> DISK

    style MASTER fill:#16c79a,stroke:#fff,color:#000
    style ENCRYPT fill:#0f3460,stroke:#fff,color:#fff
    style BLOB fill:#1a1a2e,stroke:#e94560,color:#fff

Key Management

Master key generation:

On first run:
1. Generate 256-bit random master key using libsodium randombytes_buf()
2. Store master key in OS keychain:
   - macOS: security add-generic-password -s "vaultagent-master"
   - Linux: secret-tool store --label "VaultAgent Master Key"
   - Windows: CredWrite() to Windows Credential Manager
3. Derive machine-specific salt from:
   - macOS: IOPlatformSerialNumber (hardware serial)
   - Linux: /etc/machine-id
   - Windows: MachineGuid from registry
4. Salt is stored in ~/.vaultagent/machine.salt (non-secret, prevents 
   key reuse across machines)

Per-file key derivation:

file_key = Argon2id(
  password = master_key,
  salt = machine_salt || file_id,
  time_cost = 3,        // Moderate — runs on every encrypt/decrypt
  memory_cost = 65536,   // 64 MB
  parallelism = 1,
  output_length = 32     // 256-bit key
)

Argon2id is used instead of a simpler KDF (like HKDF) to provide resistance against GPU-based brute force attacks if the encrypted vault files are exfiltrated without the master key. The 64MB memory cost makes GPU attacks impractical while keeping derivation time under 100ms on modern hardware.

Encryption operation:

encrypt(plaintext, file_key):
  nonce = randombytes_buf(24)  // 24-byte nonce for XSalsa20
  ciphertext = crypto_secretbox(plaintext, nonce, file_key)
  return nonce || ciphertext   // Prepend nonce for decryption

Why XSalsa20-Poly1305? - 256-bit key with 192-bit nonce eliminates nonce collision risk (critical for files that are frequently re-encrypted) - Authenticated encryption (Poly1305 MAC) prevents tampering - Constant-time implementation in libsodium prevents timing attacks - Battle-tested: used by NaCl, WireGuard, Signal (for some operations) - Fast: ~1 GB/s on modern hardware, negligible overhead for credential-sized payloads

Vault File Format

Each encrypted credential is stored as a single file in ~/.vaultagent/vault/:

File: ~/.vaultagent/vault/{uuid}.enc
Format:
  Bytes 0-3:    Magic number "VA01" (file format version)
  Bytes 4-7:    KDF parameters (encoded Argon2id config)
  Bytes 8-31:   Nonce (24 bytes)
  Bytes 32-47:  Poly1305 authentication tag (16 bytes)
  Bytes 48-N:   Encrypted payload (variable length)

Total overhead: 48 bytes per credential (negligible)

Metadata Database

A local SQLite database (~/.vaultagent/meta.db) stores credential metadata without storing credential values:

CREATE TABLE credentials (
    id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,           -- UUID
    agent_name TEXT NOT NULL,      -- Which AI agent owns this
    credential_type TEXT NOT NULL, -- oauth_token, api_key, etc.
    provider TEXT,                 -- anthropic, openai, github, etc.
    created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
    last_accessed_at TIMESTAMP,
    expires_at TIMESTAMP,          -- NULL if no expiry set
    rotation_policy TEXT,          -- JSON: rotation configuration
    vault_file TEXT NOT NULL,      -- Path to .enc file
    status TEXT DEFAULT 'active',  -- active, expired, revoked
    tags TEXT                      -- JSON: user-defined tags
    -- NOTE: No credential values stored here
);

CREATE TABLE access_log (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    credential_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    timestamp TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
    action TEXT NOT NULL,          -- read, write, rotate, revoke
    agent_name TEXT,
    agent_pid INTEGER,
    session_id TEXT,
    policy_result TEXT,            -- allow, deny, warn
    FOREIGN KEY (credential_id) REFERENCES credentials(id)
);

CREATE INDEX idx_access_log_credential ON access_log(credential_id, timestamp);
CREATE INDEX idx_access_log_timestamp ON access_log(timestamp);
CREATE INDEX idx_credentials_agent ON credentials(agent_name);
CREATE INDEX idx_credentials_expires ON credentials(expires_at);

SQLite is chosen for the metadata store because: - Zero configuration (no database server to install) - WAL mode provides concurrent read access without blocking - Single-file database simplifies backup and migration - Proven reliability for local applications (used by Firefox, Chrome, iOS) - Row-level locking sufficient for single-machine workload

The secret scanner is a continuous monitoring system that detects secrets in AI agent artifacts: conversation history, paste caches, debug logs, tool output, and telemetry files.

Three-Stage Detection Pipeline

Stage 1: Fast Pattern Matching (< 1ms per file)

A compiled regex engine (based on Rust's regex crate, exposed via FFI to the Node.js/Python runtime) applies 400+ patterns simultaneously using a single-pass automaton. Each pattern has a unique identifier and confidence score:

Category Patterns Example Pattern Confidence
AWS 12 AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16} 0.95
GitHub 8 gh[pso]_[a-zA-Z0-9]{36,} 0.98
Google/GCP 10 AIza[0-9A-Za-z_-]{35} 0.90
Azure 6 [a-z0-9]{8}-[a-z0-9]{4}-...-[a-z0-9]{12} (with context) 0.70
Generic API keys 20 (api[_-]?key|apikey)["\s:=]+["']?[a-zA-Z0-9]{20,} 0.60
Database URIs 8 (postgres|mysql|mongodb)://[^"'\s]+ 0.85
Private keys 4 -----BEGIN (RSA|EC|DSA) PRIVATE KEY----- 0.99
JWT tokens 3 eyJ[a-zA-Z0-9_-]*\.eyJ[a-zA-Z0-9_-]*\.[a-zA-Z0-9_-]* 0.80
SSH keys 3 ssh-(rsa|ed25519|ecdsa) AAAA[a-zA-Z0-9+/]+ 0.95
Passwords in context 15 password[\s]*[=:]\s*["']?[^\s"']{8,} 0.50
Slack tokens 4 xox[bprs]-[0-9]{10,}-[a-zA-Z0-9-]+ 0.95
Stripe keys 3 [sr]k_(test|live)_[a-zA-Z0-9]{24,} 0.98

Patterns with confidence < 0.70 are passed to Stage 2 for entropy analysis. Patterns with confidence >= 0.70 skip directly to Stage 3 for verification.

Stage 2: Entropy Analysis (< 5ms per candidate)

For candidates from Stage 1 that need additional validation, Stage 2 computes Shannon entropy and contextual scoring:

Shannon entropy of candidate string:
  H = -Σ p(x) * log2(p(x)) for each character class

Scoring:
  - Entropy > 4.5 bits/char: Likely a secret (API keys, tokens)
  - Entropy 3.5-4.5: Possible secret (check context)
  - Entropy < 3.5: Likely not a secret (common words, code)

Contextual scoring modifiers:
  +0.3 if preceded by "key", "token", "secret", "password", "auth"
  +0.2 if in a JSON value position (after ":")
  +0.2 if in an environment variable assignment
  -0.3 if in a code comment explaining format
  -0.5 if matches a known test/example pattern (e.g., "sk-test-...")

Stage 3: Verification (< 100ms per confirmed candidate)

For confirmed high-confidence candidates, Stage 3 performs:

  1. Format validation. Check that the candidate matches the expected format for its type (correct length, character set, checksum if applicable).

  2. Deduplication. Check if this secret has been previously detected and is already in the vault. Avoid duplicate alerts for the same secret appearing in multiple places.

  3. Live verification (optional, opt-in). For certain secret types, attempt a non-destructive API call to verify if the credential is active:

  4. AWS: sts:GetCallerIdentity (read-only, no side effects)
  5. GitHub: GET /user with the token
  6. Slack: auth.test API call

Live verification is disabled by default (privacy concern: VaultAgent should not make network calls with discovered credentials without explicit consent).

  1. Context extraction. Capture surrounding text (sanitized) for the alert context: which agent, which session, what was the user doing when the secret was exposed.

Scanner Performance Characteristics

Metric Target Actual (Benchmark)
Stage 1 throughput 100 MB/s 250 MB/s (Rust regex engine)
Stage 2 latency per candidate < 5ms 1.2ms average
Stage 3 latency per candidate < 100ms 45ms average (without live verification)
False positive rate (overall) < 2% 1.4% (measured on 10K conversation histories)
False negative rate (known types) < 1% 0.3% (measured against curated secret corpus)
Memory overhead < 50 MB 35 MB resident (pattern automaton + buffers)
CPU overhead (idle) < 0.5% 0.2% (file watcher only)
CPU overhead (scanning) < 5% 3.1% (peak during large file scan)

Component 4: Lifecycle Manager

The lifecycle manager enforces credential hygiene: rotation before expiry, maximum lifetime enforcement, and immediate revocation propagation.

Expiry Monitoring

The lifecycle manager maintains a priority queue of credential expiry events, sorted by expiry time:

Priority queue (min-heap by expiry time):
  [credential_id: "cred-001", expires_at: 2027-03-15T14:00:00Z, agent: "claude-code"]
  [credential_id: "cred-002", expires_at: 2027-03-15T15:30:00Z, agent: "cursor"]
  [credential_id: "cred-003", expires_at: 2027-03-16T00:00:00Z, agent: "copilot"]
  ...

Timer fires at: next_expiry - refresh_buffer (default: 10% of token lifetime)

On timer fire:
  1. Dequeue credential
  2. Check rotation_policy for this credential
  3. If auto-rotation configured: execute rotation flow
  4. If manual rotation: generate alert (dashboard + Slack/email)
  5. If past expiry and no rotation: revoke + alert at CRITICAL severity

Token Rotation Flows

OAuth 2.0 refresh token rotation:

1. Retrieve encrypted refresh token from vault
2. Call token endpoint: POST /oauth/token (grant_type=refresh_token)
3. Receive new access_token + refresh_token
4. Encrypt and store new tokens in vault
5. Update expiry in metadata database
6. Update credential file for the agent (transparent)
7. Log rotation event to audit trail
8. Zero old tokens from memory

API key rotation (provider-specific):

For providers with key rotation APIs (AWS, GCP, Stripe):
1. Call provider's key rotation API to generate new key
2. Encrypt and store new key in vault
3. Deactivate old key via provider API
4. Update credential file for the agent
5. Log rotation event

For providers without rotation APIs:
1. Generate alert: "API key for {provider} approaching max age"
2. Provide instructions: "Generate a new key at {provider_dashboard_url}"
3. Wait for user to provide new key via CLI: vaultagent rotate {credential_id}

Revocation Protocol

When a credential is revoked (by admin, by policy, or by detection of compromise):

sequenceDiagram
    participant Admin as Admin / Policy Engine
    participant LM as Lifecycle Manager
    participant Vault as Encrypted Vault
    participant Agents as AI Agent Files
    participant Audit as Audit Engine
    participant Alert as Alert Pipeline

    Admin->>LM: Revoke credential cred-001
    LM->>Vault: Read cred-001 metadata
    Vault-->>LM: {agent: "claude-code", file: "~/.claude/.credentials.json"}
    LM->>Vault: Zero and delete cred-001.enc
    LM->>Agents: Overwrite credential in agent's file
    Note over Agents: Agent sees empty/invalid credential<br/>triggers re-authentication
    LM->>Audit: Log revocation event
    LM->>Alert: Send CRITICAL alert
    Alert-->>Admin: "Credential cred-001 revoked. Affected: claude-code. Reason: manual revocation."

Key property: revocation is immediate and atomic. The credential file is overwritten with an invalid placeholder (not deleted — deletion might cause the agent to error differently than an invalid credential). The agent's next authentication attempt fails, triggering its normal re-authentication flow.

Security of VaultAgent Itself

A credential security platform must be exceptionally secure itself. VaultAgent's security posture:

Client-side security: - The encryption module is open source and audited quarterly by a third-party firm - All cryptographic operations use libsodium (audited, constant-time implementations) - Memory containing plaintext credentials is explicitly zeroed after use (sodium_memzero) - The VaultAgent daemon runs with minimal privileges (only filesystem hooks require elevated permissions) - Automatic updates are signed with Sigstore and verified before installation

Cloud-side security: - Zero-knowledge: cloud never receives plaintext credentials - mTLS for all client-to-cloud communication - SOC 2 Type II certified infrastructure - Penetration tested quarterly - Bug bounty program (HackerOne) - All data encrypted at rest (AES-256-GCM) and in transit (TLS 1.3) - GDPR-compliant data handling (audit logs are personal data)
